questions.stem: Article 1 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) states that men are:
options: born and remain free and equal in rights
born subjects of the king and of the Church
equal in rights only if they own property
free once they have paid their feudal dues
questions.explanation: Article 1 declares that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, and that social distinctions may be based only on common utility. It rejected the society of orders in which rights depended on birth.

questions.stem: Article 3 of the Declaration of the Rights of Man states that 'the principle of all sovereignty resides essentially in the nation'. This principle directly challenged:
options: the claim that the king held sovereign power in his own right
the right of citizens to own property free from interference by the state
the idea that laws should apply equally to all citizens
the authority of elected deputies to make laws for France
questions.explanation: Placing sovereignty in the nation denied the absolutist claim that sovereignty belonged to the king. It strengthened, rather than challenged, the authority of the nation's elected representatives.

questions.stem: Which statement about the Declaration of the Rights of Man is accurate?
options: It declared property an inviolable and sacred right but said nothing of women's rights
It gave the vote to every adult man and woman who paid any direct tax
It abolished slavery in France's Caribbean colonies, including Saint-Domingue, from August 1789
It made Catholicism the state religion and banned other forms of worship
questions.explanation: Article 17 calls property 'inviolable and sacred', and the Declaration was silent on women and on colonial slavery. Slavery was abolished only in 1794, and the Declaration protected religious opinions rather than imposing one faith.

questions.stem: Louis XVI delayed his approval of the August Decrees and the Declaration of the Rights of Man until October 1789. What made him finally accept them?
options: The Champ de Mars massacre, which turned the National Guard against him
The October Days, when a Paris crowd marched to Versailles and brought him to Paris
The Flight to Varennes, after which the Assembly suspended him from his royal functions
The declaration of war on Austria, which forced him to unite the nation
questions.explanation: On 5–6 October 1789 a crowd led by Parisian market women marched on Versailles over bread and the king's delays. Louis accepted the decrees and the royal family was taken to the Tuileries in Paris. The other events came in 1791 and 1792.

questions.stem: In November 1789 the National Assembly placed Church lands at the disposal of the nation. Its main purpose was to:
options: back a new paper currency, the assignats, and pay off the state's debts
give the land free of charge to peasants who had no land of their own
return the land to the nobles from whom it had been taken centuries before
fund a war against Austria that the Assembly had already declared
questions.explanation: Church property was used to back the assignats, at first bonds and then paper money, to deal with the debt that had caused the crisis. The lands were sold, mostly to bourgeois and better-off peasants, not given away; war came only in 1792.

questions.stem: Under the Civil Constitution of the Clergy (July 1790):
options: all priests were to be expelled from France within a year
priests and bishops were to be elected and paid by the state
the Pope was given the power to appoint every bishop in France
the Church kept its lands but lost its right to collect taxes
questions.explanation: The Civil Constitution reorganised dioceses to match the departments and made clergy elected, salaried officials. Bishops were no longer to seek the Pope's approval of their appointment, which is why Rome condemned it.

questions.stem: Why is the clerical oath of November 1790 often seen as a turning point of the revolution?
options: It led the Assembly to restore the tithe and the Church's lost lands
It split clergy and faithful, giving the counter-revolution popular support
It united the clergy behind the revolution and ended royal opposition to reform
It persuaded the Pope to accept the Civil Constitution of the Clergy
questions.explanation: Clergy had to swear to the Civil Constitution; roughly half refused. The division between constitutional and refractory priests split parishes and turned many devout Catholics, and the king, against the revolution. Pope Pius VI condemned the Civil Constitution in 1791.

questions.stem: The Le Chapelier Law of June 1791 affected urban workers by:
options: banning workers' associations and strikes
setting a minimum wage for Paris artisans
guaranteeing every worker a job on public works
giving workers the vote in national elections
questions.explanation: The law banned associations of workers and employers alike, including combinations to raise wages, reflecting the Assembly's belief in economic liberty. It left workers with less power to bargain.

questions.stem: The Constitution of 1791 divided citizens into 'active' and 'passive' citizens. This distinction meant that:
options: only men paying a set level of direct tax could vote
only nobles and clergy could hold public office
all adult men voted, but women had to be passive
only Paris residents could vote in national elections
questions.explanation: Active citizens were men who paid direct tax equal to at least three days' local wages; others, and all women, were passive citizens with civil rights but no vote. Critics such as Robespierre attacked this as a betrayal of equality.

questions.stem: Why was the Flight to Varennes (June 1791) so damaging to the constitutional monarchy?
options: His escape attempt implied he rejected the new constitution
The king was killed during the escape, leaving no heir to the throne
The king reached Austria safely and declared war on France
The king was crowned emperor by the Assembly on his return
questions.explanation: Louis was recognised and stopped at Varennes, and he had left a statement criticising the revolution's work. Trust in him collapsed and calls for a republic grew, although the Assembly kept him on the throne by claiming he had been abducted.

questions.stem: At the Champ de Mars on 17 July 1791, Lafayette's National Guard fired on a crowd that had gathered to:
options: celebrate the anniversary of the storming of the Bastille
demand the abolition of the Civil Constitution of the Clergy
protest against the declaration of war on Austria
sign a petition calling for the king's removal after Varennes
questions.explanation: The crowd had gathered to sign a petition, promoted by the Cordeliers, for the king's removal. The shooting split the revolutionaries and badly damaged Lafayette's standing with Parisian radicals. The war began only in April 1792.

questions.stem: In 1791–92 the Girondins (Brissotins) pushed for war against Austria. Which argument did they use?
options: War would spread liberty and expose the king and other traitors
War would bring France new colonies to replace Saint-Domingue
War would let the king restore his full powers over the Assembly
War would end the need to sell Church lands to pay the debt
questions.explanation: Brissot and his allies argued that a war of liberty would rally the nation and force traitors, including the court, into the open. Robespierre opposed them, warning that armed missionaries are not welcome. The king also favoured war, hoping defeat would restore his power.

questions.stem: The Brunswick Manifesto (July 1792) threatened Paris with destruction if the royal family were harmed. What was its effect?
options: It led the king to join the Jacobins in defending the capital
It deepened suspicion of the king and helped provoke the rising of 10 August
It persuaded the Assembly to restore Louis XVI's absolute powers to calm the Prussians
It ended the war, as France accepted the Prussian demands
questions.explanation: The threat seemed to confirm that the king was in league with the enemy. On 10 August 1792 armed Parisians and fédérés stormed the Tuileries, and the monarchy was suspended. The manifesto had the opposite effect to the one its authors intended.

questions.stem: The National Convention, elected after the fall of the monarchy, abolished the monarchy and declared France a republic in:
options: September 1792
July 1789
June 1791
July 1794
questions.explanation: The Convention met on 20 September 1792, abolished the monarchy and began Year I of the Republic on 22 September. July 1789 was the Bastille, June 1791 Varennes and July 1794 the fall of Robespierre.

questions.stem: What were the September Massacres of 1792?
options: The shooting of petitioners by the National Guard
The drowning of rebels in the Loire at Nantes
The killing of prisoners in Paris jails amid fear of invasion
The execution of the Girondin deputies after their arrest in June
questions.explanation: With Prussian forces advancing and Verdun fallen, crowds killed prisoners in Paris jails, many of them common criminals, fearing a plot by prisoners. The shooting of petitioners was the Champ de Mars in 1791; the Nantes drownings came in 1793–94.

questions.stem: Louis XVI was tried by the National Convention and executed in:
options: January 1793
October 1789
August 1792
July 1794
questions.explanation: The Convention found Louis guilty of conspiring against the nation and voted for death; he was guillotined on 21 January 1793. He had been deposed after 10 August 1792. Marie Antoinette was executed in October 1793.

questions.stem: The revolt in the Vendée in March 1793 was triggered mainly by:
options: the execution of Marie Antoinette
the closing of the Jacobin Club
the Law of 22 Prairial
the levy of 300,000 men for the army
questions.explanation: The call-up of 300,000 men for the army in February 1793 sparked revolt in a region already angered by the treatment of its priests. The other events came later in 1793–94 or after Thermidor.

questions.stem: The Federalist revolts of 1793 in cities such as Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux were mainly a reaction to:
options: the Flight to Varennes and the suspension of the king
the expulsion of the Girondin deputies in June 1793
the abolition of the monarchy and the execution of Louis XVI
the Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the clerical oath
questions.explanation: When Parisian sans-culottes forced the arrest of Girondin deputies on 2 June 1793, many provincial authorities rose against Jacobin Paris. The rebels were mostly republicans opposing Parisian domination rather than royalists, though Toulon went on to hand its port to the British.

questions.stem: Which combination of events best explains why the Convention turned to emergency government in 1793?
options: Foreign war, the Vendée revolt, Federalist risings and food shortages at once
The death of Robespierre, the Thermidorian Reaction and the end of the Maximum
The Flight to Varennes, the Champ de Mars and the 1791 Constitution
The Tennis Court Oath, the Bastille and the night of 4 August
questions.explanation: In 1793 the Republic faced war on its frontiers, civil war in the west, revolt in major cities and price rises in Paris all at once. This explains the creation of bodies such as the Committee of Public Safety. The other combinations belong to other years.

questions.stem: The Committee of Public Safety, created in April 1793, became:
options: the court that tried the king for treason
the club that organised the October Days
the body that drafted the Declaration of Rights
the effective government of France during the Terror
questions.explanation: The Committee, whose members came to include Robespierre and Saint-Just, directed the war effort, policy and repression. The king was tried by the Convention itself, and suspects by the Revolutionary Tribunal.

questions.stem: The Law of Suspects (September 1793) allowed:
options: the conscription of every unmarried man between 18 and 25
the sale of émigré lands in small lots to poorer peasants
suspected hoarders to be fined but never imprisoned
the arrest of anyone thought hostile to the revolution
questions.explanation: The law defined suspects so broadly, including those whose conduct or words showed them to be enemies of liberty, that huge numbers could be imprisoned. Conscription was the levée en masse of August 1793.

questions.stem: Why did the Convention introduce the General Maximum in September 1793?
options: To raise taxes on the clergy to pay for the war
To limit how many deputies each department could elect
To meet sans-culotte demands for controls on the prices of basic goods
To protect landowners by setting a minimum price for grain and flour
questions.explanation: The Maximum fixed maximum prices for bread and other necessities, and also wages, answering pressure from Parisian sans-culottes. It ran against the earlier revolutionary faith in free trade, showing how circumstances reshaped policy.

questions.stem: The levée en masse of August 1793:
options: abolished the army and replaced it with local National Guards
exempted married men and all peasants from military service
made the whole population liable for service to the war effort
allowed every citizen to elect the members of the Convention
questions.explanation: The levée en masse declared all French people permanently requisitioned for the war: young unmarried men to fight, others to make arms, supplies and bandages. It produced a mass army that turned the war in France's favour.

questions.stem: In February 1794 Robespierre described terror as that without which virtue is powerless, and virtue as that without which terror is fatal. What did he mean?
options: Virtue and terror were opposites, and the Republic must choose one
Terror was justified only against foreign armies, never against citizens
Terror was a necessary weapon of a virtuous republic against its enemies
Terror should be ended now that the republic had defeated its enemies
questions.explanation: Robespierre presented terror as an emanation of virtue: prompt, severe justice that a republic of virtue needed while under threat. He was justifying the Terror, not calling for its end; that was the Indulgents' position.

questions.stem: The Law of 22 Prairial (June 1794) is associated with the 'Great Terror' because it:
options: made the Terror the order of the day for the first time
applied the Terror only to nobles and refractory priests
removed defence counsel and allowed only acquittal or death
abolished the Revolutionary Tribunal and freed most suspects
questions.explanation: The law stripped the accused of counsel, allowed conviction on moral proof and gave the Tribunal only two verdicts, and executions in Paris rose sharply in June and July 1794. 'Terror the order of the day' was proclaimed in September 1793.

questions.stem: Historians agree that most people executed during the Terror were:
options: foreign prisoners of war captured on the frontiers
not nobles or clergy, but ordinary members of the Third Estate
nobles who had remained in France after 1789
refractory priests deported from the western provinces
questions.explanation: Although the Terror targeted the 'aristocratic plot', most victims were peasants, workers and bourgeois, many from rebel regions such as the Vendée and Lyon. Nobles and clergy were a minority of those executed.

questions.stem: Which was a feature of the de-Christianisation campaign of 1793–94?
options: Catholicism was made the only lawful religion
Churches were closed and turned into Temples of Reason
The tithe was restored to fund the constitutional clergy
Refractory priests were given back their parishes
questions.explanation: In autumn 1793, militants and representatives on mission closed churches, removed religious symbols and held festivals of Reason; a festival was held in Notre-Dame in November 1793. The tithe had been abolished in 1789.

questions.stem: The revolutionary calendar, adopted in 1793, counted Year I from:
options: the storming of the Bastille in July 1789
the meeting of the Estates-General in May 1789
the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793
the founding of the Republic in September 1792
questions.explanation: The calendar dated a new era from the Republic's founding on 22 September 1792, and it replaced saints' days and Sundays with ten-day weeks and names drawn from nature. It was part of the attempt to replace Christian time with republican culture.

questions.stem: Robespierre introduced the Cult of the Supreme Being in 1794. How does this relate to de-Christianisation?
options: He saw atheistic de-Christianisation as dangerous and offered a civic religion
He launched de-Christianisation and used the cult to close the remaining churches
He used the cult to restore Catholicism as the official religion of the Republic
He shared the Hébertists' atheism and designed the cult to promote it
questions.explanation: Robespierre condemned militant atheism as divisive and immoral and believed a republic needed belief in a Supreme Being and the immortality of the soul. The Festival of the Supreme Being in June 1794 replaced the Hébertists' cult of Reason; it did not restore Catholicism.

questions.stem: The sans-culottes were:
options: the moderate deputies who sat on the right in the Convention
Parisian shopkeepers, artisans and workers active in the sections
nobles who had fled abroad and formed armies against France
peasants of the west who rose against conscription
questions.explanation: The sans-culottes, named for wearing trousers rather than breeches, were mostly small shopkeepers, artisans and journeymen who dominated the Paris sections and demanded price controls and harsh measures against enemies. The émigrés and Vendéans were their opponents.

questions.stem: Which change in 1793–94 best shows the declining power of the sans-culottes under the revolutionary government?
options: The decree that made the Terror the order of the day
The execution of the Hébertists and the curbing of the sections
The passage of the General Maximum on prices and wages
The expulsion of the Girondin deputies from the Convention
questions.explanation: The Maximum, the purge of the Girondins and 'Terror the order of the day' were all sans-culotte demands that the Convention met. By spring 1794 the Committee had executed the Hébertists, tamed the sections and enforced the wage maximum, reducing popular power.

questions.stem: Jean-Paul Marat influenced the revolution mainly through:
options: his command of the Paris National Guard at the Champ de Mars in July 1791
his leadership of the Girondins in the Legislative Assembly
his drafting of the Constitution of the Year III in 1795
his newspaper 'L'Ami du peuple', which demanded action against traitors
questions.explanation: Marat's paper 'The Friend of the People' denounced traitors and called for violence against them, and it won him great popularity in Paris. He was assassinated by Charlotte Corday in July 1793 and became a revolutionary martyr. He was a fierce enemy of the Girondins.

questions.stem: Georges Danton was executed in April 1794 mainly because:
options: he was found to have helped the king escape to Varennes
he led the Federalist revolt in Lyon against the Convention
he opposed the creation of the Revolutionary Tribunal in 1793
as a leader of the Indulgents he called for an end to the Terror
questions.explanation: Danton, a leading figure in 1792–93, came to favour moderation, and with Desmoulins the Indulgents urged relaxing the Terror. The Committee saw this as a threat and had them executed, weeks after the Hébertists.

questions.stem: How did the Marquis de Lafayette's role change between 1789 and 1792?
options: From royalist general to Jacobin leader and president of the Convention
From Paris mayor to member of the Committee of Public Safety
From émigré leader abroad to commander of the Vendée rebels
From hero of 1789 to fugitive who fled to the Austrians in 1792
questions.explanation: Lafayette commanded the National Guard in 1789 but lost popular support after the Champ de Mars. As an army commander he condemned the Jacobins, and after the fall of the monarchy he crossed to the Austrians, who imprisoned him.

questions.stem: Maximilien Robespierre fell from power on:
options: 2 June 1793
13 Vendémiaire Year IV (5 October 1795)
9 Thermidor Year II (27 July 1794)
10 August 1792
questions.explanation: Deputies who feared they would be the Terror's next victims turned on Robespierre on 9 Thermidor; he was guillotined the next day. 10 August 1792 was the fall of the monarchy and 2 June 1793 the purge of the Girondins.

questions.stem: What did the women of Paris achieve during the October Days of 1789?
options: They closed the Jacobin Club and ended the Terror
They secured the abolition of the Civil Constitution
They forced the king to accept the decrees and move to Paris
They won the right to vote in elections to the Convention
questions.explanation: The women's march brought the king's acceptance of the August Decrees and the Declaration and moved the royal family, and then the Assembly, to Paris. Women never gained the vote during the revolution.

questions.stem: In 1791 Olympe de Gouges wrote the 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen'. Which was the revolutionaries' response to women's political activity by late 1793?
options: Women's political clubs were banned, and de Gouges was executed
Women gained the vote in elections to the National Convention
Women were admitted as members of the Committee of Public Safety
Women's clubs were funded by the state to support the war effort
questions.explanation: In October 1793 the Convention banned women's political clubs, including the Society of Revolutionary Republican Women, and de Gouges was guillotined in November. Women did gain civil rights such as divorce in 1792, but no political rights.

questions.stem: Which change brought the greatest lasting benefit to peasants by 1793?
options: The return of the tithe to support the parish priests
The General Maximum's requisitioning of their grain
The levy of 300,000 men to fill the armies
The abolition of remaining seigneurial dues without compensation
questions.explanation: In July 1793 the Convention abolished the remaining seigneurial dues outright, ending the redemption payments set in 1789. Requisitioning and conscription were burdens that provoked peasant resistance, and the tithe was never restored.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the experience of the nobility from 1789 to 1795?
options: They lost privileges and titles; many emigrated and had property seized
They kept their titles but lost their land to the peasants in 1789
They were all executed during the Terror as enemies of the Republic
They gained new privileges in return for supporting the Constitution of 1791
questions.explanation: Nobles lost fiscal and seigneurial privileges in 1789 and hereditary titles in 1790; many emigrated, and émigré property was confiscated. Some nobles were executed, but most survived the Terror and many stayed in France.

questions.stem: Which group is most often judged to have gained most from the revolution by 1795?
options: The bourgeoisie, through careers open to talent and national land sales
The urban workers, through a permanent wage rise and the right to strike
The refractory clergy, through the restoration of Church lands and tithes
The nobility, through compensation for their lost dues and titles
questions.explanation: Middle-class men gained equal access to office, a political voice under property-based franchises, and many bought Church and émigré land. Workers lost the Maximum's protection after Thermidor and had been banned from striking in 1791.

questions.stem: Which was a feature of the Thermidorian Reaction after Robespierre's fall?
options: The sans-culottes took control of the Convention
The Law of 22 Prairial was extended to the provinces
The Jacobin Club was closed and the Maximum abolished
The Committee of Public Safety gained new powers
questions.explanation: The Thermidorians closed the Jacobin Club in November 1794 and abolished the Maximum in December, after which prices soared. They dismantled the machinery of the Terror rather than extending it.

questions.stem: The Constitution of the Year III (1795) restricted democracy compared with the Constitution of 1793 by:
options: abolishing elections and handing power to the Committee of Public Safety
restoring property qualifications for electors and dividing power
giving the vote to every adult man and woman over the age of twenty-one
restoring Louis XVI's brother to the throne as a constitutional monarch
questions.explanation: The Constitution of 1795 created a five-man Directory and two councils and required property qualifications for electors, to prevent both dictatorship and popular rule. The democratic Constitution of 1793, with universal male suffrage, was never put into effect.

questions.stem: The 'thesis of circumstances' explains the Terror mainly as:
options: a response to the emergency of foreign war and counter-revolution
the inevitable result of ideas of popular sovereignty present from 1789
a plot by Robespierre to make himself king of France
a policy forced on the Convention by the Pope and the émigrés
questions.explanation: The thesis, associated with historians in the republican and Marxist tradition such as Georges Lefebvre, presents the Terror as a defensive reaction to war, civil war and crisis. François Furet, by contrast, argued that the Terror grew out of revolutionary political culture from 1789.

questions.stem: Historian François Furet challenged the Marxist interpretation of the revolution mainly by arguing that:
options: revolutionary ideas and political culture, not class struggle, drove events, including the Terror
the revolution was a bourgeois revolution that destroyed feudalism and opened the way to capitalism
the Terror was caused entirely by the war and would not have occurred in peacetime
the sans-culottes were the true leaders of the revolution from 1789 to 1795
questions.explanation: Furet emphasised the dynamics of revolutionary discourse, such as the claim to speak for the people and the hunt for enemies, which he saw as leading to the Terror. The bourgeois-revolution thesis is the Marxist view of Lefebvre and Soboul that he attacked.
